title: The Midlife Crisis Question: Are You Changing, or Trying to Escape?
author: Camilo Zambrano
summary: Camilo Zambrano starts from a conversation with a friend nearing forty who feels trapped at work and newly aware of the finiteness of time, and asks why people reconsider their lives in middle age. He draws on Laura Carstensen's socioemotional selectivity theory, which holds that our goals shift with our perceived time horizon rather than our chronological age. He warns against confusing change with escape, using the Eat, Pray, Love trend as an example of treating someone else's journey as a universal blueprint, and notes that confirmation bias and cognitive dissonance can make a crisis spiral. Decisions made earlier were made with the information then available, and their consequences remain. His answer draws on the Stoics: acknowledge fear instead of eliminating it, act on what is within your control, and practice returning to your principles after drifting, which builds self-governance. He recommends a circle that challenges rather than validates you.
points: Priorities change as people perceive less time ahead, which explains why many reassess their lives near midlife.
Dissatisfaction can fuel meaningful change or an impulse to escape, and treating another person's story as a blueprint risks needless chaos.
Hindsight distorts past choices, and the consequences of earlier decisions and responsibilities do not disappear when our perspective shifts.
Stoic practice means acknowledging fear and focusing on what is within your control rather than trying to eliminate it.
Self-governance grows through the skill of returning to your principles quickly after drifting, with a circle that challenges rather than validates you.
quotes: In many cases, this helps us pursue a more meaningful life, leading to lasting changes that really mark a difference between who we were and who we are. Other times, this dissatisfaction can lead to an overwhelming desire to escape.

Discovering that something no longer matters as much doesn’t mean it was a mistake to pursue it in the first place, and I think that’s one of the particular issues we face when we fall into a crisis like a midlife crisis.
The thing we tend to forget is that the decisions we made in the past were made with the information we had at hand, not with the information we hold today. Hindsight is 20/20.
Essentially, if we think we have little time, or that our loved ones have little time, that influences what matters.
When we mistake someone else’s journey of self-discovery for a universal blueprint for our own lives, we risk bringing unwarranted chaos into our lives for the sake of a temporary escape.
The best thing we can do, by knowing our nature — something I learned from the Stoics — is to acknowledge the instinct and allow ourselves to feel it, so we can take control of ourselves again.
In the end, self-governance isn’t only about choosing what serves you today; it involves recognizing the responsibilities and consequences that remain from yesterday’s choices.
